title: Economy and Civics
lines: This topic tests basic ideas of economics and government, common abbreviations, and international bodies. USAT asks for meanings of terms, the job of an institution, or what an abbreviation stands for. Numbers that change, such as growth rates or budgets, are not asked.
## Basic economics
| Term | Meaning
| GDP | Gross Domestic Product: value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a year
| GNP | Gross National Product: GDP plus net income earned by citizens abroad
| Per capita income | national income divided by population
| Inflation | a general rise in prices, which lowers the buying power of money
| Deflation | a general fall in prices
| Fiscal policy | government taxing and spending, set through the budget
| Monetary policy | central bank control of money supply and interest rates
| Budget deficit | government spending greater than revenue
| Balance of trade | exports minus imports of goods
| Balance of payments | record of all transactions with the rest of the world
| Direct tax | paid by the person on whom it falls, e.g. income tax
| Indirect tax | passed on through prices, e.g. sales tax, customs duty
- Law of demand: when price rises, quantity demanded falls (other things equal). Law of supply: when price rises, quantity supplied rises.
- Devaluation lowers a currency's value against others, making exports cheaper and imports dearer.
## Government and the state
- Four elements of a state: population, territory, government and sovereignty.
- Three organs: the legislature makes laws, the executive carries them out, and the judiciary interprets them and settles disputes. Montesquieu argued for separation of these powers.
| System | Feature | Example
| Federal | power divided between centre and provinces or states | Pakistan, USA
| Unitary | power held mainly by the centre | United Kingdom, France
| Parliamentary | government answers to the legislature; head of state and head of government are separate | Pakistan, UK
| Presidential | president is both head of state and government, elected separately | USA
- Democracy is rule by the people through elected representatives. A constitution is the basic law that sets up the state. Franchise is the right to vote.

## International bodies and their roles
- IMF: short-term loans to countries with balance-of-payments problems. World Bank: long-term loans for development projects.
- WTO: rules for international trade and settling trade disputes.
- International Court of Justice: disputes between states, at The Hague.
> A government raises income tax and cuts its own spending to control inflation. This is an example of  (A) monetary policy  (B) fiscal policy  (C) trade policy  (D) devaluation
> B. Taxes and government spending are fiscal tools. Monetary policy works through interest rates and money supply, set by the central bank.
> Sales tax is an example of  (A) a direct tax  (B) an indirect tax  (C) a wealth tax  (D) a property tax
> B. The seller collects sales tax and passes it on to the buyer through the price.
## Traps
! Fiscal policy belongs to the government; monetary policy to the central bank (the State Bank in Pakistan).
! GDP counts production inside the country; GNP adds net income from abroad.
! The IMF lends for balance-of-payments support; the World Bank lends for projects. Do not swap them.
## Quick check
- GDP, inflation, fiscal versus monetary policy, direct versus indirect tax.
- Elements of a state; three organs; federal versus unitary; parliamentary versus presidential.
- NADRA, HEC, WAPDA, FBR, SECP, PEMRA.
- IMF, World Bank, WTO, ICJ: who does what.
